source: Groenendijk (2012, thesis ch.2) describing Getzels and Csikszentmihalyi (1976) The Creative Vision
finding: Founding paradigm. Fine art students composed and drew a still life under lab conditions. Problem finding was coded at two stages: while arranging objects (problem formulation) and while drawing (problem solution).
numbers: Formulation stage: number of objects handled, interaction with the objects, uniqueness of chosen objects. Solution stage: how long the problem stayed open, exploratory behaviour (switching medium, sketches), changes from arrangement to final work. Drawings photographed every 6 minutes; students interviewed afterwards.
limits: Second-hand description in a Dutch thesis, not the 1976 book. Other sources give the sample as 31 students and 27 objects; this text does not.
agent_relevance: A measurable proxy for problem finding is behaviour before commitment (how much is explored, how long the frame stays open). Our program can log the same things: number of reframes tried, time before a frame is fixed, changes from first to final framing.

source: Groenendijk (2012, thesis ch.2) on Getzels and Csikszentmihalyi (1976)
finding: Both stages of problem finding correlated positively with rated creativity. Students who kept the problem open and explored while drawing made work judged more creative and original than students who fixed the problem early. Interviews: high scorers gave the objects personal meaning and had no finished picture in mind at the start.
numbers: Direction of effect only; no coefficients in this source. Book p.95 is quoted for colours and shapes unfolding before the eyes changing the meaning of the work.
quote: colours and shapes unfolding before their eyes
limits: Correlational, one art-school sample, one task; the book's own statistics were not read.
agent_relevance: Supports S1 and open mode: the frame should stay revisable while output accumulates, and an early fixed picture of the answer is the risk.

source: Groenendijk (2012, thesis ch.2) citing Oostwoud Wijdenes (1983)
finding: A study of secondary school students on artistic tasks found that some of them do not engage in problem finding at all.
numbers: No numbers given in this source.
limits: Only a one-sentence report; original not opened.
agent_relevance: Problem finding is not automatic even for able people. Without a slot that forces it, an agent may skip it entirely, as these students did.

source: Abdulla (2016, dissertation, UGA) reporting Csikszentmihalyi and Getzels (1971)
finding: Five well-known artists and art critics rated each drawing on craftsmanship, originality (regardless of craft) and overall aesthetic value. Discovery-oriented behaviour at the problem-formulation stage correlated with originality.
numbers: r = .54, p < .01 between concern for discovery at the formulation stage and originality. Total problem-formulation score also correlated 'highly' with originality (value not given in this source).
limits: Reported second-hand; the sample size is not stated in this source. The craftsmanship result is not given.
agent_relevance: The one hard number from the founding study: about r = .5 with originality. Useful as the expected size when we test whether a reframe slot raises distinct valid outputs. It is a correlation, so it does not show that forcing exploration causes originality.

source: Abdulla (2016, dissertation, UGA) reporting Moore (1982)
finding: Moore (1982) repeated the Csikszentmihalyi and Getzels design with adolescent writers instead of artists. Five judges rated the written products. A high-creativity group did better on originality.
numbers: N = 8 high-creative vs 8 low-creative adolescents. Problem finding defined as how problems are suggested, posed, formed, envisaged or credited. Problem finding related to product originality.
limits: Tiny groups. Exact statistics not given in this source. Same research tradition and same judge-panel format as the original.
agent_relevance: One small extension from art to writing. Domain transfer is plausible but thin; the meta-analysis later puts writing as the strongest domain (r = .36).

source: Wakefield (1991) Problem Finding and Empathy in Art (ERIC ED335259) on Getzels and Csikszentmihalyi (1976)
finding: Describes the study as a longitudinal one begun at the Art Institute of Chicago in 1963. Quotes a student in the upper third on problem finding who chose a chunk of optical glass as the key element and said it 'distorts what passed behind it'. The authors read the glass as a symbol of the artist's own way of distorting reality.
numbers: Book pages cited: 144-145. The same student said he 'felt exposed by being watched'.
limits: Case example, not data. Wakefield uses it to argue that problem finding starts from conflicting feelings.
agent_relevance: Affective and personal framing is part of how humans find problems. Our agent has no such source; the nearest substitute is an explicit statement of what the asker is trying to achieve and what conflicts in the task.

source: Wakefield (1991) Problem Finding and Empathy in Art (ERIC ED335259)
finding: Theory proposal. Artists find problems by empathy with oneself: problems begin as descriptions of conflicting feelings within the artist. Supporting evidence is preliminary: artists' reports in earlier creativity studies, Faulkner and van Gogh, and stories told by creative college students to the blank card of the Thematic Apperception Test.
numbers: TAT blank card: students described the imagined picture and told a story in one go. Ratio of blank-card to picture-card response length used as a creativity index; fine-arts majors were more responsive to the blank card than other education majors.
limits: Hypothesis plus informal data. No sample sizes in the passages read. Not a test of causation.
agent_relevance: The blank card is a useful pattern: an input with no given problem forces the model to supply its own. It can be a probe for open mode (what problem does the model pose when none is posed).

source: Getzels (1975, 1982) as summarized in Abdulla (2016) ch.2
finding: Core theory. Presented problems have a known formulation, known method and known solution. Discovered problems have none of the three. Getzels (1982) lists 10 situations that vary whether the problem is given, exists but is unidentified, or does not yet exist, and whether a method is known to the solver and to others.
numbers: 10 problem situations; the DISCOVER model (Maker et al., 2006) later reuses the problem/method/solution continuum.
quote: the problem does not yet have a known formulation, there is no known method of solution, and no known solution
limits: Typology, not tested. Terms overlap and later work found no empirical difference by label (see a19).
agent_relevance: A clean way to tag a task for the schema: is the problem given, identifiable, or to be invented? Only the last two should open S1.

source: Abdulla (2016) citing Dillon (1982, 1988) and Arlin (1975, 1977)
finding: Dillon proposed three levels: recognition, discovery and invention of the problem or solution. Arlin (1975) said problem finding needs a problematic situation, a chance to raise questions in it, and a way to categorise the questions; she called it a post-formal stage that older people should do better.
numbers: Arlin's age prediction is tested by the meta-analysis: children r = .297, adolescents r = .113, adults r = .207 (see a18).
limits: Theory papers. Arlin's developmental claim was not supported by the meta-analysis.
agent_relevance: The three-part recipe (situation, chance to ask, a way to sort questions) maps onto an open-mode slot: generate questions, then sort them in code.

source: Runco and Okuda (1988) Problem discovery, divergent thinking, and the creative process; read via Abdulla (2016) and Abdulla Alabbasi et al. (2021)
finding: Adolescents did three divergent thinking tests, each with presented problems and one self-discovered problem. Discovered problems drew significantly more ideas than presented ones. Scores on the two kinds of problem were only moderately correlated. Discovered-problem scores tied to creative performance.
numbers: N = 29 (19 male, 10 female) adolescents. Presented vs discovered correlation r = .32. Authors: problem finding is 'by definition statistically independent' of problem solving.
quote: Problem discovery is a particularly important component in the creative process because it occurs first
limits: Small N. Second-hand reading. 'Independent' rests on a moderate but significant correlation.
agent_relevance: Discovering your own problem produces more ideas than being handed one. That fits an open mode where the model chooses the question, and it warns that scores on given tasks will not predict it.

source: Okuda, Runco and Berger (1991) Creativity and the finding and solving of real-world problems; abstract via Claremont repository
finding: Four tasks were given to elementary school students with a checklist of creative activities as the outcome. A real-world problem-finding task predicted creative accomplishments better than divergent thinking tasks or a real-world problem-solving task. In hierarchical regression it added significant prediction beyond the others.
numbers: N = 77 elementary school students; 4 tasks. No coefficients on the page read.
limits: Abstract page only; criterion is a checklist of creative activities. Journal of Psychoeducational Assessment 9, 45-53.
agent_relevance: Problem finding may carry predictive information that solving scores miss. For evaluation, include a problem-posing probe, not only answer accuracy.

source: Wakefield (1985) Towards creativity: problem finding in a divergent-thinking exercise (ERIC ED253987)
finding: Blank cards were inserted into Pattern Meanings and Line Meanings so children could draw their own pattern and respond to it. Responses to the child's own drawings correlated with a creativity attitude scale (GIFT) but not with intelligence. The reverse held for presented drawings.
numbers: N = 23 fifth graders. Reliability of the creative performance score .82 (Spearman-Brown). Divergent thinking score vs WISC-R Vocabulary r = .45. A later review cites r = .75 between figural DT and PF. Hypotheses tested one-tailed at .05 and .01.
quote: freedom to discover and solve problems appears to be the primary condition of creative performance
limits: Tiny, above-average, single school; one-tailed tests; only fluency scored.
agent_relevance: Self-posed items load on creativity and given items load on intelligence. Open-mode output quality should be judged on its own scale, not with a given-task benchmark.

source: Hoover (1994) scientific problem finding, as reported in Abdulla (2016)
finding: In gifted fifth graders, scientific problem finding (forming hypotheses) was more related to flexibility than to fluency on the Torrance tests.
numbers: N = 40 (18 male, 22 female). Flexibility r = .41; fluency r = .34.
limits: Second-hand. Small gifted sample.
agent_relevance: Flexibility (shifting category of idea) tracks problem finding more than quantity of ideas. Argues for category-diverse reframes over many reframes of one type.

source: Getzels and Smilansky (1983) as reported by Abdulla Alabbasi et al. (2021)
finding: High school students formulated problems about school. Verbal originality and flexibility were weakly tied to problem-finding quality; verbal fluency was not. No figural score related to problem finding.
numbers: Verbal originality r = .23; verbal flexibility r = .18; fluency not significant; figural fluency, flexibility and originality all not significant.
limits: Small coefficients. Reported through a 2021 review.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition: the link between divergent thinking and problem finding depends on task type, and is weak in school-age samples. Idea fluency is not a stand-in for good framing.

source: Arlin (1975), Artley et al. (1980), Lee and Cho (2007), Ambrosio (1994) as reported by Abdulla Alabbasi et al. (2021)
finding: Mixed and sometimes negative links between divergent thinking and problem finding. Arlin: quality of problems related positively to adaptive flexibility, negatively to fluency. Lee and Cho: DT and problem finding in ill-structured situations were negatively related. Ambrosio: DT related to quantity of problems found but not to quality.
numbers: Arlin: adaptive flexibility r = .26, spontaneous flexibility r = -.09, fluency r = -.18. Artley: verbal fluency r = .47. Lee and Cho: r = -.17. Ambrosio: quantity r = .41, quality r = -.08.
limits: Different tests, ages and scorings; quality vs quantity scoring flips the sign and is the main moderator.
agent_relevance: Counting how many problems an agent raises is a poor measure. Quality of the problem is a separate axis and may even run the other way.

source: Abdulla, Paek, Cramond, Runco meta-analysis, as reported in Abdulla (2016) Chapter 3
finding: Problem finding and creativity are moderately and significantly correlated across 40 studies, with very high heterogeneity.
numbers: Random effects r = .22 (95% CI .11 to .32); fixed effects r = .39 (.38 to .40). k = 40 studies, 6,649 participants, 196 effect sizes. Q(195) = 15,480.27, p < .001, I2 = 98.74%. Studies 1960-2015, published and unpublished.
limits: I2 near 99% means the mean is a poor summary. Effects are mostly correlations with divergent thinking tests, not with real-world accomplishment. The published version (Psychology of Aesthetics, Creativity, and the Arts 14(1)) was not opened.
agent_relevance: Expect a modest, variable gain from any problem-finding step. Do not assume large effects; plan to measure per domain.

source: Abdulla (2016) Chapter 3, publication-bias checks
finding: The meta-analysis found signs of small-study asymmetry. One huge near-perfect outlier pulled the mean up.
numbers: Egger intercept t = 5.52, p < .001. Rosenthal fail-safe N = 6,414. Removing Frederiksen and Ward (1978), r = .99 with N = 2,636, drops the mean from .220 to .196. Trim-and-fill not used because of heterogeneity.
limits: Egger test is unreliable with this much heterogeneity. Fail-safe N is a weak guide.
agent_relevance: Treat .22 as an upper-ish estimate; .20 or lower is a safer planning value.

source: Abdulla (2016) Chapter 3, moderator analyses
finding: Three moderators mattered: age, divergent thinking index, and domain. Gender and the type of creativity measure did not. Children showed stronger links than adolescents, against Arlin's post-formal idea.
numbers: Age Q(2) = 6.60, p < .03: children r = .297, adolescents .113, adults .207. DT index Q(3) = 10.95, p < .01: fluency .314, originality .291, flexibility .149. Domain Q(4) = 18.44, p < .001: writing .360, art .199, science/math .162, social/humanities .091. Gender Q(2) = 1.69, p = .47 (female .305, male .183). Creativity measure Q(3) = 0.65, p = .88 (product .248, personality .230, problem solving .204, DT .196).
limits: Some CIs are very wide (fluency -.084 to .625; social/humanities -.213 to .379). Cells are small. Domain is confounded with the instrument. The dissertation gives two female/male figures in different places (.305/.183 and .293/.183).
agent_relevance: Writing tasks show the strongest tie, art weaker, science and math weakest. An open-mode reframing slot is most likely to help on open-ended writing-like tasks and least on closed math tasks.

source: Abdulla (2016) Chapter 2, systematic review of terms
finding: At least 13 labels are used for problem finding across about 199 works, and the ANOVA in the meta-analysis found that the label did not change study results. Fields prefer their own label (problem posing in math, hypothesis formulation in science).
numbers: Share of works: problem finding 50.3%, problem posing 12.1%, problem construction 9.5%, problem formulation 9.1%, ill-defined problems 4%, problem generation 3.1%, others 2.5% or less.
limits: Counts come from title and abstract searches in seven databases, so they are not the whole literature.
agent_relevance: When we search literature or write prompts, use all labels; no single word covers the field.

source: Abdulla and Cramond (2018) Creative Problem Finding Hierarchy, as described in Abdulla (2016) ch.2 and Wikipedia
finding: A proposed five-level scheme: discovery, formulation, construction, identification, definition. Levels differ by how ill-defined the problem is and by how much ideation versus evaluation is needed. Discovery is the most ill-defined and ideation-only; definition is mostly evaluative.
numbers: Two dimensions, five processes. Wikipedia (opened, secondary) lists the same five with brief definitions.
limits: The author says the hierarchy is new and untested. No data.
agent_relevance: Closest thing to a spec we can code. Discovery and formulation are ideation steps with no early critic (in line with G1); definition and identification are evaluative steps that code can run.

source: Abdulla Alabbasi, Reiter-Palmon, Sultan, Ayoub (2021) Which divergent thinking index is more associated with problem finding ability? Frontiers in Psychology 12:671146
finding: Verbal flexibility tracked problem finding much more than fluency or originality. Figural tasks tracked it far less. Verbal flexibility predicted problem-finding fluency, flexibility and originality in path models.
numbers: N = 90 sixth graders. Verbal: flexibility r = .71-.76, fluency .68-.71, originality .55-.61. Figural: originality .27-.31, flexibility .15-.20, fluency .14-.18. Variance explained: 40-58% verbal, 28-37% figural. Problem Generation test: 235, 253, 269 distinct problems on the three tasks.
limits: One age group, one country; the same group built the tests. The Problem Generation test lists problems, it does not frame a given problem.
agent_relevance: Language-based problem finding is easier to measure and tracks flexibility. That fits an LLM, whose world is verbal. Suggests scoring reframes by category diversity.

source: Reiter-Palmon, Mumford, O'Connor Boes, Runco (1997) Problem construction and creativity: the role of ability, cue consistency, and active processing. Creativity Research Journal 10(1)
finding: Problem construction ability predicted solution quality and originality. It interacted with cue consistency: high-ability people did better when the problem's cues were inconsistent. Instructions could raise active engagement in construction.
numbers: N = 195 undergraduates; 6 real-life problems; solutions rated for quality, originality, creativity.
limits: Only the repository abstract page was read, so effect sizes are missing; the PDF returned 403. The benefit is conditional on the person and on the cues.
agent_relevance: Reframing helps most when the inputs conflict. That is a signal for G1: trigger a reframe when cues disagree or checks fail, not on every task.

source: Reiter-Palmon and Murugavel (2018) The effect of problem construction on team creativity. Frontiers in Psychology 9:2098
finding: Teams told to restate the problem before solving it gave solutions that were only marginally more original, with no gain in quality. Teams that did the restating reported less conflict and more satisfaction.
numbers: 195 participants in 65 teams of three, 4 conditions (3 construction variants, 1 control); 19 control and 46 construction groups after pooling. Originality F(1,63) = 2.06, p = .078, eta squared = .03. Quality no difference. The three instruction types did not differ: originality F(2,43) = 0.56, p = .578; quality F(2,43) = 0.68, p = .513.
limits: The abstract says 'more original ideas' but the effect is marginal. F = 2.06 with df 1,63 gives p about .16 two-sided by my calculation; the paper's .078 looks one-sided. Student teams, one task.
agent_relevance: A small and shaky effect from forced problem restatement. Treat the restate step as cheap, not as a main lever, and test it before relying on it.

source: Mumford, Reiter-Palmon, Redmond (1994) problem construction model, via Reiter-Palmon and Murugavel (2018) and Abdulla (2016)
finding: Model: problem construction is built from stored problem representations. It mostly happens automatically and people are unaware they are defining a problem. Active construction through instructions raised creativity of solutions in earlier studies, and quality and originality of the construction predicted quality and originality of the solution.
numbers: No new numbers; the model rests on Mumford et al. (1993, 1994, 1996) and Reiter-Palmon et al. (1997).
quote: schematic, or categorical, knowledge structures abstracted from prior problem-solving efforts
limits: The chapter itself was not opened (no open copy found). The stored representations are the same schemas that cause set effects in experts.
agent_relevance: The mechanism: framing comes from stored schemas. For an LLM that means training-data priors. Reframing must pull in a schema from a different place, otherwise it is the same frame again.

source: Csikszentmihalyi and Getzels (1988), quoted in Abdulla (2016) ch.2
finding: Authors' view of the process: problem finding is metacognitive and involves affect and motivation as well as logic. The review adds that discovery may be unconscious and knowledge-dependent.
numbers: Page 92 of the 1988 chapter.
quote: metacognitive in the sense that they involve unconscious or preconscious affective and motivational elements as well as logic
limits: Quote only; the chapter was not opened.
agent_relevance: Problem finding cannot be derived from logic alone. A scaffold can supply the logic around it (listing, sorting, checking) but the seed of a new frame needs a source the program cannot generate.

source: Wikipedia (2026 snapshot) Problem finding
finding: Secondary summary. Cites Runco and Nemiro (1994) and Abdulla and Cramond (2018); attributes distinctions to Basadur (discovery vs formulation), Runco and Chand (identification vs definition) and Pretz, Naples, Sternberg (problem finding applies to ill-defined problems).
numbers: No empirical numbers.
limits: Encyclopedia page, not a source for claims. Used only to check names and citations.
agent_relevance: A pointer list for the angle-B and angle-C agents; not evidence.

source: Longitudinal claims about the art students (Getzels and Csikszentmihalyi 1976; 1988 follow-up) as reported in web summaries
finding: Web summaries say the 31 students were tracked later: problem finders were more likely to still be working as artists and were judged more successful. Intelligence did not correlate with studio performance or later success.
numbers: Summaries conflict. Follow-up counts: 27 of 31 found at 5 years (one source), all 31 (another). 8 of the 11 lowest problem finders had quit art (one source). Other sources say 7 and 18 years. Task: 27 objects, 1 hour.
limits: NOT opened: the MIT Reader page returned access denied; figures come from search snippets and must be checked against the book or the 1988 chapter before use.
agent_relevance: The headline that finders stayed in art is cited everywhere but is unverified here. Do not quote the 8/11 or 27/31 figures until the original is read.

source: Sinhahajari, Majumder, Poria (2026) On the limits of LLM-as-judge for scientific novelty assessment (RQ-Bench), arXiv 2606.12071
finding: Research-question generation is a prerequisite for ideation. LLM judges rated model-generated research questions as more novel than the questions authors actually asked (a 'novelty mirage'). Domain experts preferred the author questions. Model questions were narrower and tied to their source papers.
numbers: 1,434 questions from 746 arXiv papers. Expert check on 50 items: experts gave the author question non-obviousness win rates of 78% and 56%; LLM judges gave gpt-5.5's best-of-five 82% (gemini-3.1-pro) and 52% (deepseek-v4-pro). Human-LLM agreement as low as 22%; expert-expert 60%, LLM-LLM 52%. Standalone, gpt-5.5 strict win rate 27.2% (non-obviousness) and 38.4% (originality). Source-boundedness score: authors 0.47, gemini 0.90, gpt-5.5 1.17; gpt-5.5 loses 71.7%, wins 4.3%.
limits: Reference questions are 'author-anchored' (reconstructed by an LLM pipeline from background, gaps and contributions), not the only valid ones. CS papers only. Expert sample of 50.
agent_relevance: Strongest direct LLM evidence: models generate research questions that look novel to LLM judges but experts find less non-obvious and too bound to the source. Agrees with G5: do not let a model judge the quality of its own reframes.

source: Mishra, Sahu, et al. (2026) AInstein: can LLMs solve research problems from parametric memory alone? arXiv 2510.05432
finding: Tests solving of given research problems, not finding them. Models solved over 70% of problems but rediscovered the published method under 19% of the time, and failed where the solution needed cross-domain analogy.
numbers: 1,214 ICLR 2025 papers (LLM judge). Blind study with N = 20 AI researchers on ICLR 2026 problems: LLM solutions preferred on solving the problem in 73.5% of decided pairs (p = 2.2e-5), on originality 65.2% (p = .006), feasibility no difference (p = .685). Mistral-24B not significant on originality (p = .30).
limits: Problem statements are extracted from papers, so this is given-problem solving. Included as the contrast case: it shows what is not problem finding.
agent_relevance: Models are decent when the problem is handed to them. The open gap is finding the problem, which this study never tests.

source: Li, Kim, Wang (2025) QuestBench: can LLMs ask the right question to acquire information in reasoning tasks? arXiv 2503.22674
finding: Underspecified problems solvable by asking one question. Models pick the right question from options well on math but poorly on logic and planning. Solving the fully specified version is not enough to know what to ask.
numbers: Four sets: Logic-Q, Planning-Q, GSM-Q, GSME-Q. Models (GPT-4o, o1-preview, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Gemini 1.5 Pro, Gemini 2.0 Flash Thinking) over 80% on GSM-Q and GSME-Q but 40-50% or lower on Logic-Q and Planning-Q.
limits: Multiple choice, one missing variable. Real problem finding has no option list. Models of early 2025.
agent_relevance: Question-asking is a separate skill from answering. The scaffold should not assume a model can name the missing piece, and where the structure allows, code should find the missing piece.

source: Li, Kim, Wang (2025) QuestBench, 'not sure' ablation
finding: When allowed to say the problem is underspecified, models rarely did on planning problems, even though many were. They tended to guess instead of flagging missing information.
numbers: Planning-Q zero-shot: Gemini Flash Thinking, Claude 3.5 and GPT-4o answered 'not sure' on only 1.4%, 4.6% and 0.7% of cases, against a true rate of 41.8%. Gains over a random baseline at most 5% on Planning-Q.
limits: Zero-shot, no chain of thought in this row. Older models.
agent_relevance: Detecting that the problem itself is incomplete is the weakest part. An external check that the frame is complete (an S1 gate) is safer than asking the model.

source: Tian et al. (2023, v4 2025) MacGyver: are large language models creative problem solvers? arXiv 2311.09682
finding: Constrained everyday problems that need unusual use of objects, with unsolvable ones included. GPT-4 often proposed solutions to problems that cannot be solved, a form of failed problem finding. On average GPT-4 beat individual humans slightly, but humans did better as a group.
numbers: 1,683 problems; 78% solvable, 22% unsolvable (377). GPT-4: 18.9% efficient solution, 37.5% infeasible solution on solvable ones. Humans N = 252 (Prolific): majority correct 79.3% vs GPT-4 73.3%. Humans varied more (perfect or fail); GPT-4 clustered in the middle.
limits: Problems were LLM-generated with human checks. GPT-4 era. Tests physical reasoning, not research problems.
agent_relevance: Model overconfidence: it will solve a problem that has no solution. A pre-solve feasibility check (S1) should be a coded gate that can return 'cannot be solved as posed'.

source: Edwards and Schuster (2026) Ask or assume? Uncertainty-aware clarification-seeking in coding agents, arXiv 2603.26233
finding: Agents on SWE-bench Verified with parts of the issue removed. Splitting out a separate step that detects what is missing raised the resolve rate to near the full-information agent. A single prompt that mixed detection and coding did worse.
numbers: Claude Sonnet 4.5: hidden-info baseline 54.8%, single-agent uncertainty prompt 61.2%, prompted interactive baseline 70.4%, multi-agent detector 69.4% (vs single p < 0.001; vs interactive p = 0.621). Kimi K2.6: single 61.6%, multi 69.4%, interactive baseline 47.2%. Sonnet asked 3.06 queries per task (multi) vs 1.84 (single).
limits: Simulated user; software tasks only; task count not confirmed in the text read.
agent_relevance: Closest scaffold result: a separate role that only looks for what is missing beats one prompt that does both. Matches our design: the program decides, a slot only fills the gap list.

source: Hu et al. (2024) Nova: iterative planning and search to enhance novelty and diversity of LLM-generated ideas, arXiv 2410.14255
finding: An idea-generation agent whose planning prompts borrow from philosophy of science: identify anomalies in existing theories (Kuhn, Laudan) as a source of new problems. Iterative retrieval raised the count of unique novel ideas.
numbers: Unique novel ideas rose 3.4 times from baseline over iterations; top Swiss Tournament score of 5 in its Figure 1. Human expert reviews used.
limits: The gain comes from iterative retrieval of outside knowledge, not from the problem-definition step alone; no ablation of the 'define new problem' prompt was read. The prompts only name the theories.
agent_relevance: Anomaly as a seed for a new problem is a code-usable trigger: find where checks fail or sources disagree, then pose that gap as the problem.

source: Search record for this angle: no LLM study found that runs the Getzels-Csikszentmihalyi paradigm or a Problem Generation test
finding: Searches (web, arXiv, Semantic Scholar, OpenAlex) found no paper that scores an LLM on the classic problem-finding paradigm (open problem, exploration before commitment, expert rating). Nearest items are RQ-Bench, QuestBench, MacGyver, Ask-or-Assume and Nova.
numbers: Several searches returned nothing relevant; web search quota ran out, and Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex returned rate-limit errors.
limits: Absence of evidence under a limited search. Do not state as fact that none exists.
agent_relevance: Our own open-mode probe would be new: give the model an input with no stated task (blank card), then compare expert ratings of the problems it poses against a plain run.
